strengths: Well-motivated and timely benchmark targeting the molecule-language interface, a genuinely underexplored gap; the paper clearly articulates why existing molecule-language datasets (ChEBI-20, L+M-24) are ambiguous and not structure-grounded.

Rigorous and transparent data curation: recognition tasks are auto-generated with RDKit from UniChem (deterministic ground truth), while editing/generation tasks go through a multi-annotator pipeline with independent validation requiring exact structural reconstruction; the pipeline and annotation standards are documented in detail.

Comprehensive and current evaluation covering many frontier models (GPT-5, o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1, chemistry-specific LLMs, and an image-generation model), including both SMILES and image modalities, with complete results, snapshot versions, variance analysis, and prompt-sensitivity/SMILES-enumeration robustness checks in the appendix.

Interesting and useful analyses beyond headline numbers: the recognition-vs-localization gap and the plausible BPE-tokenization explanation (with a concrete worked example), per-edit-category error breakdowns, and a pragmatic OCR-based semi-automated evaluation for image outputs, all reported honestly.

Findings are clear and actionable (e.g., near-random performance on E/Z classification for most models, ~43% generation accuracy for the best model, near-zero image-generation accuracy), and the dataset and code are released.
weaknesses: Small evaluation sets: only 200 instances per task, which limits statistical power for the many per-task and per-category comparisons drawn (e.g., per-edit-category accuracies on 1-3 samples in Table S2 are unreliable).

No quantitative human baseline: the paper repeatedly claims these tasks are 'intuitively simple for humans' and frames model failures relative to human ability, but no human evaluation is actually conducted or reported.

Recognition task design partially conflates chemical understanding with convention-following: localization accuracy depends on models reproducing a specific atom-indexing convention defined in the prompt, so part of the failure may be instruction-following rather than structural reasoning; the BPE-tokenization explanation is speculative and not empirically verified.

Evaluation is restricted to closed, mostly proprietary frontier APIs; open-source general LLMs and graph-language multimodal models are essentially absent (graph models are acknowledged but not attempted), which limits breadth and reproducibility of results over time.

The editing/generation task setup is somewhat artificial relative to the motivating chemist workflows: molecules capped at <40 heavy atoms, at most two modifications per instruction, and no consideration of synthetic feasibility or property constraints, so real-world significance of the 43.0%/85.5% numbers is hard to gauge.

Data-contamination risk is not addressed: models like GPT-5 may have seen UniChem-derived SMILES during pretraining; the claim that 'newer models do better, therefore the benchmark is well-annotated' is a weak validation argument and contamination could inflate recognition results.

Image-based editing/generation evaluation relies on a small manually validated subset plus a commercial OCR tool with unquantified conversion accuracy; the false-positive analysis covers only 200 samples and the protocol is fragile.

Presentation issues: several typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'the GPT-5 achieves', 'still fail', broken dataset/code links in footnotes, mislabeled Figure 4 example description, garbled Figure S2), and the related-work section is relatively thin on differentiation from recent chemistry benchmarks such as ChemBench, MatSci-adjacent efforts, and text-to-molecule generation benchmarks.

strengths: The three tasks (recognition, editing, generation) reflect genuine chemist workflows and the emphasis on deterministic, unambiguous answers is a sensible design principle that addresses a real weakness of prior molecule-text datasets (e.g., ChEBI-20, L+M-24).
The multi-stage human annotation/validation pipeline with independent reconstruction checks is thorough and well-documented, including useful annotation statistics and cost accounting.

Broad evaluation coverage across many current LLMs, reasoning models, and vision-language models, with useful auxiliary analyses (prompt sensitivity, variance across runs, OCR-based automated evaluation, tokenization failure analysis).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper is a fairly incremental benchmark in a crowded space. Prior work (Text2Mol, MolT5, L+M-24, Mol-Instructions, ChEBI-20, chemistry QA benchmarks) already covers molecule-language recognition, captioning, and generation; the incremental contribution over these is narrower structure-grounded tasks, which is a modest delta.

Very small benchmark scale: only 200 instances per task (18 recognition subtasks, one editing task, one generation task). With 200 examples per cell, accuracy differences of a few points (e.g., GPT-5's 85.5% vs. o3's 78.5% editing) are within plausible sampling noise, yet the paper draws strong rankings from them; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are provided.

Only commercial closed-source models (GPT family, DeepSeek APIs) are meaningfully evaluated on the main tasks; the chemistry-specific open models tested fail almost entirely due to format compliance, suggesting the benchmark mostly measures instruction following of proprietary frontier models rather than molecular capability. No fine-tuning experiments or baselines (e.g., fine-tuned open models on the provided auxiliary data) are included to demonstrate the benchmark can drive progress.

The claim of 'comprehensive' and multi-representation support is overstated: the graph modality is never evaluated (footnote 2), and the image editing/generation side is evaluated only with a single model (GPT Image 1), with effectively zero accuracy—raising questions about whether the image generation portion is informative at all.

Recognition tasks are already near-saturated for the strongest model (86-92%), meaning the benchmark may rapidly lose discriminative power; only stereochemistry remains hard, and several subtasks are arguably artificial (e.g., 3-hop neighbor enumeration by index is a proxy task unlikely to appear in real chemical workflows and may primarily measure tokenization/counting artifacts as the paper itself admits).

Potential contamination and difficulty calibration are not addressed: SMILES from UniChem/PubChem are extremely likely in the training corpora of the evaluated models, and the paper provides no de-duplication or decontamination analysis, nor any human baseline to substantiate the claim that tasks are 'intuitively simple for humans.'

Evaluation methodology for the generation task conflates multiple failure modes (validity, scaffold, substituent placement, stereochemistry) into a single all-or-nothing 43% number, limiting diagnostic value; no partial-credit or fine-grained error breakdown is offered in the main text.

Significance and actionability are limited: the paper identifies that models fail, but offers little toward closing the gap—no training data released beyond a small auxiliary set (which the paper itself notes is expensive to scale), no analysis of what interventions would help.

strengths: High-quality, rigorously validated benchmark construction: the multi-stage annotation pipeline (independent annotators, peer review, and two independent validators who must reconstruct the molecule from the instruction/description) directly addresses the ambiguity problem that plagues prior molecule-description datasets (e.g., ChEBI-20, Text2Mol). Requiring exact structural match via canonical SMILES/InChIKey gives deterministic, objective ground truth.

Comprehensive task design: 18 recognition subtasks spanning local topology, functional groups, and stereochemistry (constructed programmatically with RDKit for guaranteed correctness), plus expert-annotated editing and generation tasks — covering a meaningful slice of real chemist workflows rather than ad hoc caption-style tasks.

Broad and current model coverage: 12+ LLMs including GPT-5, o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1, and image-generation models, evaluated across both SMILES and image modalities, with complete per-task results, model snapshot documentation (Table S3), and variance analysis over repeated runs.

Genuinely insightful analyses: the recognition-vs-localization accuracy gap traced to BPE tokenization (Appendix A.11, analogous to the 'strawberry' counting failure), sub-random performance on E/Z stereochemistry, prompt sensitivity tests (SMILES enumeration, terminology rephrasing), and the OCR-based semi-automated evaluation of generated images with careful validation of its false-positive rate.

Clear, honest reporting of limitations (absence of graph-language evaluation, annotation cost, inability to scale manually), and release of dataset/code plus an auxiliary training set supports reproducibility and future work.

The headline findings are actionable and well-supported: even GPT-5 achieves only 43% on generation and ~86% on recognition tasks that are trivial for humans, quantifying a real gap at the molecule-language interface.
weaknesses: Benchmark size is modest: 200 core instances per task (plus a less rigorously validated extended set). For recognition tasks, 200 examples per subtask limits statistical resolution for distinguishing close models; confidence intervals or significance tests across models are not reported.

Evaluation is confined to zero-shot prompting of closed-source API models (except R1-70B). There are no fine-tuned baselines, no tool-augmented/agent baselines (e.g., LLM + RDKit function calling, which could plausibly solve many recognition tasks), and no investigation of few-shot or chain-of-thought variants — limiting our understanding of what is needed to close the gap the benchmark identifies.
The paper markets graph representation support, but no graph-language models are actually evaluated (footnote 2), so one of the three advertised modalities is effectively untested.

Some results invite deeper follow-up but receive only brief treatment: e.g., chemistry-specific LLMs fail almost entirely (A.7) with limited error analysis, and the image-generation evaluation (GPT Image 1) rests largely on manual judgment of a single commercial model.

Potential contamination/memorization risk is not discussed: UniChem-sourced molecules and GPT-5's strong relative performance leave open whether some familiarity with common structures inflates recognition scores.

Editing instructions limited to at most two modifications, and molecules restricted to <40 heavy atoms, narrow the practical difficulty range; the claim that tasks reflect real chemist workflows would be strengthened by harder, multi-step instances.

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark that targets a genuine gap: existing molecule-language datasets (e.g., ChEBI-20, Text2Mol) use ambiguous descriptions, while MolLangBench enforces deterministic, uniquely-correct answers via a rigorous multi-annotator/multi-validator pipeline, which is a meaningful methodological contribution for the molecule-language domain.

Comprehensive coverage of three task types (recognition, editing, generation) and three molecular modalities (SMILES, images, graphs), making the benchmark broadly reusable for LLMs, VLMs, and graph-language models.

Extensive evaluation of ~18 frontier models including GPT-5, o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-R1, and Claude-Opus-4.1, with complete per-task results, variance/pass@k analysis, prompt-sensitivity studies, and SELFIES comparisons, lending credibility and reproducibility to the reported numbers.

Genuinely insightful analyses: the recognition-vs-localization gap and the BPE tokenization hypothesis (Appendix A.18), error taxonomy for editing/generation (Table 3), the structure-first prompting improvement on BBBP/BACE, and the demonstration that chemistry-specific and graph-language models underperform general LLMs.

High annotation quality controls (independent validation with exact structural matching, discard-on-failure policy, documented annotation statistics and time costs) plus a canary string and auxiliary training set; dataset and code are released.
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale: only 200 core instances per task (plus a lighter-validation extended set), and molecules restricted to <40 heavy atoms; this raises statistical-power concerns for fine-grained comparisons and limits coverage of realistic drug-like complexity.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior molecule-language benchmarks (ChEBI-20, Text2Mol, L+M-24, chemistry Q&A benchmarks); the core contribution is curation rigor and a new task decomposition rather than new methods or scientific insight, and several headline findings (LLMs struggle with stereochemistry, atom enumeration, and exact SMILES generation) confirm what is largely already suspected.

Evaluation is zero-shot prompting of closed-source APIs only, with no fine-tuning or tool-augmented (e.g., RDKit-assisted) baselines, so the benchmark does not yet demonstrate that it can drive or measure progress, only that current models fail; the long-term utility of requiring models to manually enumerate atom indices (localization accuracy) is debatable, since this conflates model ability with an unnatural interface.

Recognition tasks are largely constructed via RDKit scripts over UniChem and may partially reflect string/token-level artifacts; potential train-set contamination of UniChem-derived molecules in LLM pretraining is only addressed via a canary string, and no decontamination analysis is provided.

Writing and presentation issues remain (e.g., missing URLs in the abstract, typos such as 'molecule-langauge', 'Sturcutre', 'Consisten'), and several claims (e.g., 'establishing a gold standard') are stronger than the evidence; the downstream property-prediction experiment uses only two non-reasoning models and two datasets.

strengths: The editing and generation datasets are curated through a rigorous multi-annotator pipeline with independent validation, ensuring deterministic and unambiguous ground truth—a genuine improvement over existing ambiguous molecule-text datasets such as ChEBI-20.

The evaluation covers a very broad and up-to-date suite of models (GPT-4o through GPT-5, o3/o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4.1, DeepSeek-R1, open-source chemistry LLMs, VLMs, and graph-language models), across three modalities (SMILES, images, graphs).

The paper includes several useful supplementary analyses: prompt-sensitivity checks, variance/pass@k analysis, error taxonomy, SELFIES comparison, tokenization-related enumeration failures, and a small experiment linking structure recognition to property prediction.

The finding that frontier models still fail substantially on molecule generation (43%) and on stereochemistry tasks is an interesting and practically relevant observation for the molecule-language interface sub-area.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: molecule-language benchmarks and evaluation of LLMs on chemical tasks already exist (e.g., Guo et al. 2023, Text2Mol/MolT5 line of work, ChEBI-20/L+M-24); the main contribution is a cleaner annotation protocol applied to a familiar task family, which is incremental.

The test sets are small (200 core instances per task; the 'extended' set of 200 was built with a deliberately simplified, single-annotator pipeline), so reported per-task accuracies carry substantial statistical uncertainty, which is not quantified (no confidence intervals or significance tests); differences of a few points between models (e.g., GPT-5 vs. Gemini-2.5-Pro) may not be meaningful.

The recognition tasks are quite synthetic: ground truth is generated by RDKit and depends on atom indices assigned by SMILES token ordering, which partially measures tokenizer artifacts and string manipulation rather than chemical understanding; the paper itself concedes this for the designed 'hard' cases.

Contamination is a real concern: molecules and canonical SMILES are drawn from UniChem/PubChem, which are likely in the training corpora of the evaluated models; the canary string does not address memorization of the underlying molecules.

Recognition appears to be saturating for frontier models (GPT-5 at 86.2% with 1.0/0.925 on several subtasks), reducing the benchmark's long-term discriminative value, while the generation task is arguably the only task with meaningful headroom.

Only zero-shot prompting is evaluated; no tool-augmented, retrieval-augmented, or fine-tuned baselines, and no human-expert baseline is quantified, making the claim that these tasks are 'intuitively simple for humans' unsupported by measurement.

The property-prediction correlation experiment (Appendix A.13) is thin—only two classification tasks, two non-reasoning models, and ~5% accuracy gains do not robustly establish the causal claim that structure recognition is a prerequisite for downstream performance.

Presentation issues undermine polish: multiple typos ('molecule-langauge', 'Consisten', 'Ring Sturcutre', 'Ommitted', 'still fail'), and the dataset/code URLs in the abstract appear as empty placeholders; the error analysis is limited to a single model (o3).

strengths: High-quality, rigorously curated benchmark: the multi-stage annotation pipeline (annotator → peer review → independent validation with exact structural reconstruction) with explicit ambiguity rejection is a strong methodological contribution that addresses a real deficiency in existing molecule-language datasets (ChEBI-20-style descriptions are often ambiguous and not structure-grounded).
Well-motivated task decomposition aligned with real chemist workflows (recognition, editing, generation), with deterministic, uniquely correct answers enabling precise automated evaluation.

Comprehensive evaluation breadth: 16+ frontier LLMs, vision-language and image-generation models, chemistry-specific LLMs (ChemDFM, ChemLLM, Galactica), and graph-language models (HIGHT, Llamole), spanning multiple input representations (SMILES, SELFIES, images, graphs).

Thorough and transparent analysis: pass@k, variance analysis, prompt sensitivity, error taxonomy, tokenization/BPE failure analysis, OCR-based automated evaluation of image outputs, dataset chemical-space coverage, and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., SELFIES underperformance).

Findings are significant and actionable: even GPT-5 achieves only 43.0% on generation and models below random on stereo recognition; the recognition-vs-localization gap traced to tokenization is a novel, verifiable insight; the property-prediction experiment (structure-first prompting improves BBBP/BACE accuracy) ties the benchmark to downstream relevance.
Reproducibility effort is above average: model snapshot versions reported, variance quantified, canary string embedded, dataset/code promised publicly.
weaknesses: Recognition tasks are partly tied to SMILES-string index conventions, so a portion of measured performance reflects tokenization/index-enumeration artifacts rather than genuine molecular understanding; the benchmark may therefore conflate distinct capability dimensions.

Small test sets (200 instances per task) limit statistical power and granularity of conclusions, especially for per-category accuracy claims (some categories contain only 1-3 samples in the core set, e.g., tautomerization).

The vision-language evaluation is narrow and OpenAI-centric (o3/o4-mini/GPT Image 1); no open-source or competing VLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL, Gemini vision) are evaluated, weakening the generality of the claim that visual representations underperform SMILES.

Only zero-shot prompting is used; no tool-augmented or agentic baselines (e.g., code execution with RDKit), which could substantially change results and are the natural deployment configuration for chemistry assistants.

Potential training-data contamination for recognition molecules sourced from UniChem is acknowledged only indirectly (canary string); no leakage probe is actually run, so reported recognition accuracy may overestimate or be confounded by memorization.
As a benchmark-only paper, it diagnoses limitations but proposes no method to address them; the practical utility depends on community adoption, which is not yet demonstrated.
